newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe to roll back state, but no "hyperliberalism".
newsitem.headline: Juppe to roll back state, but no "hyperliberalism".

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe pledged on Tuesday to roll back the state and press ahead with tax and spending cuts, but ruled out a shift to "the simplistic hyperliberalism of the 1980s".

Presenting his campaign platform for an early parliamentary election, he stressed continuation of current policies rather than radical change, while seeking to unite all wings of the centre-right coalition behind him.
"The existence in our majority of a liberal tendency, a Gaullist tendency and a Christian-Democratic tendency is a strength.
"But there is also a time to unite. At the time of launching the battle, the general interest of the country must predominate over all other considerations," he said.
He reaffirmed France's commitment to launching a single European currency on time in 1999, saying the new euro must be on an equal footing with the dollar and the yen.

"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union and everything to gain from Europe," he said. "(We need) the euro now, because afterwards it will be too late."

Economists said his campaign speech confirmed their view the government was seeking a mandate to continue current policies, while putting France in a strong negotiating position ahead of the launch of European monetary union.

"It's not a change in policy, but more a referendum on current policy, perhaps with a little acceleration on spending cuts," said Jean-Louis Mourier, an economist at Louis Dreyfus Finance. "The ultraliberal option pushed by some...has been rejected."
Juppe, whose two-year-old government has presided over a steady rise in unemployment to a record 12.8 percent, said that the fight for jobs "has been, is and will remain our obsession".
The economy was beginning to create more jobs, he said, but these were not enough given a rise in the active working population.
The answer was not to create public-sector jobs and cut working hours -- both proposals of the opposition Socialist party -- but to encourage investment and free enterprise.
He pledged the government to reduce charges on companies.
Its current programme of lowering income taxes and social security charges would be continued and amplified.

And this would mean further public spending cuts to clear the way for lowering taxes, he said, echoing comments made by President Jacques Chirac when he announced on Monday he was calling the two-round parliamentary election for May 25 and June 1.
France must "redefine the role of the state in the national economy, notably by continuing privatisations," he said.
But there would no big swing to unfettered capitalism. "The selfish individualism, vulgar capitalism and simplistic hyperliberalism of the 1980s have gone out of fashion," he said.

Some analysts had suggested previously that Chirac might use the election to shift towards more free-market policies, bringing back into the government ultraliberals like former finance minister Alain Madelin, fired by Juppe in August 1995.

But economists say they now believe Chirac and his government, assuming the centre-right wins, will tend more to gradual reform over the five-year life of the new parliament, albeit with a slightly more liberal twist.

Juppe stressed in his speech the records not just of his own government but also that of his predecessor Edouard Balladur, another gradual reformer who earned Chirac's wrath by running against him in 1995 presidential elections.
Economists believe some Balladur supporters may be brought into the new government in a spirit of reconciliation.
